extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history (general and scholarly) interested in religion, morals, and antiquity
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-historical treatment of ancient and early-medieval beliefs in miracles, oracles, exorcisms, and juridical/practical norms relating to slaves and religious practice. The text discusses how historians and contemporaries judged authenticity and credibility of such phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of Royal and Public Miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria and practices by which contemporaries and later writers accepted public miracles (e.g., the royal 'touch' for scrofula): medical attestation, public ceremony, clerical sanction, and official registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A surgeon of the royal household attested diseases before miracles; the king touched the sick and placed a riband with a gold coin round the neck of the person touched; an official register was kept of the persons touched (John Brown, Charisma Basilicon, and Macaulay’s account of Charles II touching tens of thousands). The rite was publicly announced and performed with divines and readings (Mark xvi). These institutional trappings and eyewitness/surgeon testimony were treated as evidence for the miracle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for Credibility of Oracles and Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principal theories explaining oracles: (1) inspiration by dæmons/spirits (Platonist/Christian account), and (2) natural causes such as vapours from caverns (Aristotelian account); decline of oracles attributed to death of dæmons or exhaustion of vapours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors weigh these rival explanations when assessing oracle-claims: Platonists/Christians accept a dæmonic intermediary; Aristotle (and later commentators) point to naturalistic causes. Plutarch, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Apuleius, and others articulate and combine these views; historians use them to explain the rise/decline of oracular credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction in Evaluating Exorcisms and Miracles (Healing vs. Prophecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early-Christian and patristic views distinguished the beneficent miracle of healing from prophetic miracles; there was debate whether dæmons could or would cure diseases they caused, and whether prescience was divine or observational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fathers often held that dæmons might cure only diseases they had caused, or that their cures used natural means; some Fathers thought intuitive prescience (true prophecy) was a Divine prerogative while dæmonic 'prescience' arose from superior observation. This distinction informs whether early exorcisms/miracles are treated as genuine or imposture (see Baltus, Bingham, Middleton, Gregory of Tours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical Standards: Comparison of Conflicting Accounts and Natural Explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of comparative source criticism and appeal to naturalistic explanations (medical, physical, or fraud) when accounts conflict or appear improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: historians note differences between Suetonius and Tacitus about miraculous cures; Pliny and Cicero offer naturalistic explanations (vapours, seeds of fire, interpretation by contraries). The text repeatedly contrasts supernatural accounts with rational explanations and cites debates among scholars (e.g., Middleton’s Free Enquiry) as models of critical historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of Patristic and Early Christian Writings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of genuineness of purported patristic documents: recognition that 'the immense number of the forged documents is one of the most disgraceful features of the Church history of the first few centuries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes noting how many alleged writings were forged, that leading fathers sometimes repeated or cited doubtful letters, and that there were almost no systematic efforts to prevent such forgeries (one recorded priest degraded). Scholarly debate (Fleury, Troplong, Aubertin, Dourif) is cited as part of assessing provenance and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for Slave Testimony and Judicial Use of Slaves' Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman legal and jurisconsult standards limiting when slaves could be called as witnesses and protecting accused persons from abuses: slaves only called in incest, adultery, murder, high treason, or where no other evidence possible; requirement of prior probability and free witnesses before subjecting slaves to torture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rules: Hadrian's requirement that the reality of the crime must have acquired strong probability; Paul’s rule that at least two free witnesses should be heard before slaves were submitted to torture; refusal to accept offers to have one's slaves tortured to attest innocence. These are presented as normative legal safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman Legal Protections and Definitions of Cruelty to Slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisconsults and later laws defined cruelty broadly and instituted protections (e.g., prohibitions on separating slave families in forced sales, right of public slaves to dispose of half their goods by will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Wallon’s examination of slave laws: maxims against separating families, custom to let public/state slaves bequeath half their goods, and jurisconsults considering degrading a literary slave to coarse labor as cruelty. These legal norms are used as criteria to judge treatment of slaves in historical accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical Ethical Claims about Slavery and Treatment of Slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical positions used as moral standards: Aristotle regarded slavery as natural but advocated humane treatment; Epicurus and others practised kindness to slaves; Stoic and other moralists urged duties toward slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites passages from Aristotle, Epicurus, Seneca, Epictetus, and Plutarch illustrating that major schools promoted humane conduct. These philosophical prescriptions serve as evaluative benchmarks for moral judgments about ancient slaveholding practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting Dreams, Omens, and Signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods and conventions for interpreting dreams and omens (e.g., taking contraries, distinguishing varieties of lightning, cultural differences in auspicious side), which shape how such phenomena are reported and evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Pliny’s suggestion that dreams be 'interpreted by contraries', the augurs’ eleven kinds of lightning with different significations, and Cicero’s obser vation that Romans/Greeks judged left/right lightning differently. Such interpretive rules explain how contemporaries understood and recorded prodigies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Institutional and Documentary Evidence in Miracle Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight given to institutional records, contemporary registers, and corroborating documentation when assessing miraculous claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the royal touch ceremonies had monthly registers and surgeon testimony; absence/presence of such documentary evidence is treated as important by historians assessing authenticity or popular belief in miracles.
